name: Philippine Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Philippine languages generally lack European-style T-V distinction. Respect is expressed through po/ho particles, pronoun choice (2nd person plural for singular formal), and vocabulary selection.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Philippine languages have no grammatical gender. Pronouns (siya/niya) are gender-neutral. No special inclusive conventions needed.

linguisticChallenges.focusSystem: Philippine languages use a voice/focus system (also called 'trigger' or 'alignment') where verbal morphology marks the semantic role of the syntactically prominent argument. This is NOT like active/passive voice — it's a fundamentally different system that most MT models handle poorly.
linguisticChallenges.spanishSubstrate: Extensive Spanish loanwords integrated into core vocabulary (numbers, days, months, food, religion, government). Code-mixing with Spanish-derived terms is the norm, not an error.
linguisticChallenges.englishCodeswitching: Taglish/Bislish/etc. (mixing with English) is ubiquitous in modern spoken and written language. Pure monolingual text can sound overly formal or archaic.
linguisticChallenges.reduplication: Productive reduplication for plurality, diminution, intensity, and aspect. Both full and partial reduplication are morphologically significant.

contactInfluences.notes: 333 years of colonization. Thousands of fully nativized loanwords.
Co-official language. Taglish/Bislish code-switching is the default register in urban areas.
Shared Austronesian vocabulary. Trade pidgin influence in southern Philippines.

notes: Genus template for Philippine Austronesian languages. All Philippine languages share the focus/trigger system, extensive Spanish/English contact influence, and Latin script.
